title: From Numbers to Meaning: High-Dimensional Embeddings
hook: Tokens are just numbers. How does an AI know that king minus man plus woman equals queen?
mental_model: 3D vector space floating in dark space. Word coordinates shifting live as vector arithmetic (+/-) pulls vectors toward 'Queen'.

loop.plan: Last line flows into the first line: '…how do these vectors talk to each other? Tokens are just numbers…'. The last frame is the same dark star-field with a lone glowing dot, which is the first frame.
loop.bait: Token 9246 returns as a tiny glowing dot hidden inside the Queen vector in Scene 4. Only people who watch twice spot it.

style: Dark space, deep blue and violet, neon cyan and gold accents, clean glowing lines, cinematic slow camera, vertical 9:16, no text baked into the video (captions are added later), no people, no logos.

substeps.text: Create a fal.ai API key that expires in 7 days: fal.ai dashboard → Keys → Add key, scope API, expiration 7 days. Name it for the short (for example day2-voice). Copy it once; you cannot see it again.
Store it in the macOS Keychain once, in your own Terminal (it asks you to paste the key, so it never appears in chat or shell history).
Dry run: prints the exact request, calls nothing, costs nothing.
Generate the voice. It saves remotion/public/S2-05-vo.wav, the word timings (assets/words.json) and the scene timing from the voice (assets/scene_timing.json).
Read the report it prints: total length at most the short's length, and no ⚠️ on a scene (a scene over about 8 s is longer than one Flow clip: speed it up or make two clips).
Free re-timing without the key or any cost (after you replace the audio yourself, or if Whisper failed the first time).
Check it in Remotion Studio: play it with sound and watch the captions follow the voice. If Studio is not running, start it first.
When the voice is final, revoke the key in the fal.ai dashboard (it also expires by itself after 7 days) and remove the Keychain item. A key must never outlive the work it was made for.
Review the result: tick ✔️ reviewed in the 📝 panel and tell Claude what to change (voice, speed, wording). Claude logs the round on 🔁 Iterations.

metadata.description: Tokens are just numbers. So how does an AI know that king minus man plus woman equals queen? In 45 seconds: embeddings turn one number into 1,536 coordinates, and meaning becomes distance. Day 2 of the series, the sequel to Day 1 (tokens). Next: how do these vectors talk to each other? 👀

why.title: Why this short matters (for you, the producer)
why.note: 🔒 Producer only, not for the audience. Claude's draft from what you told me: correct it, it drives every later decision.

points.principle: Attention is the scarce thing, and the platform measures one question: did they stay, and did they come back?
points.meaning: At 200%+ watch time every view counts as two. That is why you love the example, and why the loop and the hidden 9246 are the product, not decoration.

points.principle: A viewer can absorb about one new idea in 45 seconds.
points.meaning: Day 2's single idea: meaning is distance. Embeddings are the bridge from Day 1 (tokens are numbers) to the next question (how do vectors talk). Cut anything that does not serve that one idea.

points.principle: A series compounds; a one-off does not.
points.meaning: Each short must sell the next one. Day 2 only works if a Day 1 viewer feels the sequel and a new viewer wants Day 3. That is the reason for the teaser and the series tie-in.

points.principle: You cannot out-spend studios; you can out-iterate them.
points.meaning: The master spec, the numbered pipeline and the feedback loop make short number 3 cheaper and better than number 2. Every round we log is a lesson reused next time.

points.principle: Your scarce resource is your own time, and Flow is manual.
points.meaning: Every minute spent in Flow must go to prompts you already approved. So review earliest and cheapest first: script (S2-01), storyboard (S2-02), prompts (S2-03), only then clips (S2-04).

Done means: you are proud to post it, the loop feels seamless on replay, the idea lands in one watch and the bait is caught on the second. Anti-goal: beautiful clips that explain nothing, or a first-time view that feels like a loop restart.

titles: How AI Knows King − Man + Woman = Queen 🤯 #shorts
AI does math with meaning (King − Man + Woman = ?) 👑 #shorts
Why 1,536 numbers make an AI understand words 🧠 #shorts

voice.tone: calm, curious, a little fast; no silence at the end so the loop is tight
voice.key_policy: short-lived fal.ai key (7 days), stored in the macOS Keychain (service fal-key) or an env var for one command, revoked when the voice is final

research.bigpicture: A language model does arithmetic, not reading. Before it can do anything with the word “king”, the word has to become numbers. An embedding is the rule for that: every token gets a long list of numbers (a point in space) arranged so that similar meanings sit close together. This one idea sits under search, chatbots, recommendations and RAG.

sections.title: Tokens are just numbers
sections.say: Tokens are just numbers. This one, nine-two-four-six, is a word. But to the AI, it means nothing yet.
sections.explain: Text is first chopped into tokens (whole words or pieces of words) and each token gets an integer ID from a fixed vocabulary. ID 9246 is only a row number in a dictionary, like a page number: it says which word it is and nothing about what the word means. 9246 is not special; it is the hidden detail the loop returns to.
sections.nuance: Real token IDs depend on the tokenizer. Our 9246 is an illustrative ID, not a claim about a specific model.

sections.title: One number becomes 1,536 coordinates
sections.say: So it gets unfolded. One number becomes fifteen hundred and thirty-six coordinates.
sections.explain: The model keeps a big table, the embedding matrix, with one row per token. Looking up ID 9246 returns that row: a vector of many decimal numbers. Each number is one coordinate, so the row is a point in a space with that many dimensions. 1,536 is a real size: OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small and ada-002 produce 1,536 numbers per text.
sections.nuance: Different models use different sizes (hundreds to thousands). The individual coordinates have no human label such as “royalty”; the meaning is in the pattern across all of them.

sections.title: Meaning becomes distance
sections.say: And meaning becomes distance. Apples, pears, grapes gather here. Kings, queens, crowns, over there.
sections.explain: The numbers are not random. They are learned during training so that words used in similar contexts end up close together. Fruit words appear around “eat”, “ripe”, “juice”; royal words appear around “throne”, “crown”, “rule”. Closeness is measured with simple geometry (distance, or the angle between two vectors, called cosine similarity). That is why a search for “cheap flights” can find “budget airfare”.
sections.nuance: We draw 2 dimensions because screens are flat. The real space has 1,536, and the picture is a squashed shadow of it.

sections.title: King − man + woman
sections.say: Now watch. Take king. Subtract man. Add woman.
sections.explain: Because directions in the space carry meaning, you can do arithmetic on meaning. “King − man” removes the male part and leaves roughly “royalty”. Adding “woman” puts a female part back. The step from man to woman is a direction, and the same step moves king to queen.
sections.nuance: This is the famous result from word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013). It works best on classic word embeddings, and the check usually skips the input words themselves when it looks for the nearest word.

sections.title: And you land on queen
sections.say: And you land exactly on queen. No one told it. It's just geometry.
sections.explain: Nobody wrote a rule “queen is the female king”. The model only practised predicting words from their neighbours across huge amounts of text. “The king wore a crown” and “the queen wore a crown” share contexts, so king and queen end up near each other, and the male-to-female step turns out to be the same step everywhere. Structure appears as a side effect of prediction.
sections.nuance: “Exactly” is dramatic license: you land very close to queen, and queen is usually the nearest word, not a perfect match. For the short we say it plainly; this page keeps the honest version.

sections.title: How do vectors talk to each other?
sections.say: But how do these vectors talk to each other?
sections.explain: An embedding gives each word a fixed starting point, but “bank” in “river bank” and “bank account” needs different meanings. The next layer, attention, lets every word's vector look at the others and pull in the context that matters. That is the Day 3 teaser, and the question loops back to the first line.
sections.nuance: Attention was introduced in 2017 (“Attention Is All You Need”). Day 3 can show it as vectors pulling on each other.

why.detail: Semantic search compares embeddings, so “car won't start” finds “engine trouble” even with no shared word.

why.point: RAG and chat with your documents
why.detail: Documents are embedded and stored; the question is embedded; the closest chunks are handed to the model. No embeddings, no RAG.
Songs, products and people can be embedded too. Nearby points are things you will likely like.

why.point: The first layer of every LLM
why.detail: Every language model starts by turning tokens into vectors. Understanding this is the entry ticket to understanding attention, transformers and everything after.

why.point: Why models are biased and how to fix it
why.detail: Directions in the space can encode stereotypes learned from text. You can only audit that if you know the space exists.
Embedding a page costs a fraction of a cent, which is why this is the most used AI building block in production.

sources.label: Mikolov et al. 2013, word2vec (king − man + woman ≈ queen)

did: Hosted the site on Fly.io (app day-2-short) and turned GitHub Pages into a redirect
One stable address for the review site. Browser-saved notes live per address, so the address must not change between rounds.
Created the Sprite day-2: a cloud computer that holds the repo and the agent CLIs
The AI agent gets a sandbox to edit and build in, so it never touches your laptop or your files.
Read agent keys from Azure Key Vault straight into memory and sent them to the Sprite on stdin only
The repo is public and some keys are short-lived. A key in a command line, file, page or chat can leak.
Wrote a local runner (scripts/notes_runner.py) that the 🚀 button calls; it listens on 127.0.0.1 only and accepts only this site's origins
A web page cannot run the sprite command by itself. The runner is the one small bridge, and nobody else on the network can reach it.
The Sprite returns a patch of source files only; the runner applies, builds, commits, pushes and deploys
No GitHub token ever goes to the Sprite. If the agent misbehaves, the worst case is a bad patch that fails the build and is reverted.
The runner refuses to start unless the repo is clean and equal to origin/main
So the patch always applies and a run never mixes with unsaved work.
Every run ends with a RESULT block: commit, push check, Fly deploy check, or the exact failing step
You can see at a glance whether it worked, and why not if it did not.
Added evals (offline, live, end to end) and an agent install check
Bugs hide where parts meet. Evals and the check found: kilo swallowing the piped script, two ports already used, a vault key returning 401, and the wrong command name for antigravity.
Fixed claude auth: it now uses your /login on the Sprite, not the vault key
The vault key was invalid and overrode your login, so the first claude run failed with Invalid API key. After the fix a real note went through.
Added a preview service on the Sprite, a local server, and trunk-based development (main only, push and deploy every time)
You can look at what the Sprite serves, run the same pages locally, and every change is a small, reversible commit.
why_video: A short lives or dies on small details: the hook, the first 2 seconds, a caption. Here a note typed while watching becomes a deployed fix in minutes, so you can review many more rounds in the time one used to take.
You stay in the creative seat
The repetitive work (rewriting prompts, timing tables, captions, checklists, copy) is done by the agent. Your time goes to what only you can judge: does it feel right, will people rewatch it.
Every change is a commit with a reason
Each fix is a commit plus an Iterations entry. You can see what changed and why, and undo any round with a revert. Scripts, prompts and specs are the video's source code.
The agent edits text and data, never media. Keys stay out of the repo and the page. The agent has no GitHub token. A failed build is reverted before anything is pushed.
Day 3 reuses the same spec, runner and checks. What broke on Day 2 is written into the spec so it does not break again.

Flow clips, the voice and the final render are still manual or slow steps. The agent only speeds up the editing of the plan around them. Kilo runs on a free model, so keep notes small and specific and read the RESULT block each time.
